The Deutsches Museum's Flugwerft Schleissheim page says the glider on display is a replica built by the museum in 1958, after the original acquired from Lilienthal's estate in 1904 had decayed; the inventory year 1976 fits the replica, not the 1904 original, so the record calls it a replica. 282k faces, 15 meshes, nine 2048 px textures plus one 512 px, 57 MB unpacked; already in metres and Y-up, 6.89 m span by 4.80 m long by 3.07 m tall as scanned. object.medium: Hang glider: willow and bamboo frame covered with waxed cotton, folding wings
object.description: The first aircraft ever produced in series and sold: Otto Lilienthal's 'normal soaring apparatus' of 1894, a hang glider of willow, bamboo and waxed cotton weighing 20 kg, which he flew from an artificial hill he built in Berlin-Lichterfelde and from the Gollenberg near Stölln. Lilienthal made some two thousand glides in his machines, the first repeated, controlled flights by a human being, and sold at least nine of this model for 500 marks each. He died on 10 August 1896, the day after a crash in one. This is a scan of the Deutsches Museum's replica, built by the museum in 1958 after the original from Lilienthal's estate had decayed.
facts: The Wright brothers began with Lilienthal's tables of lift; the 1903 Flyer in the next row is where his line of work led.
Buyers of the production glider included Nikolai Zhukovsky in Moscow and the publisher William Randolph Hearst; originals survive in London, Washington and Moscow.
The pilot hung by the forearms in the frame and steered by swinging the body; the wings fold for transport, and a bow at the front cushioned crashes.
